card.keepWhy: Keep throwing. The good soil makes up for all of it.
sources: Matthew 13:1-3 (great crowds; Jesus sits in a boat, the multitude stands on the beach; he speaks to them in parables: “Behold, a farmer went out to sow”)
Matthew 13:4-7 (seed on the road, devoured by birds; on rocky ground, sprang up and was scorched because it had no root; among thorns, which choked it)
Matthew 13:8 (good ground: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, some thirty)
Matthew 13:9 (“He who has ears to hear, let him hear”)
Matthew 13:18-23 (Jesus explains: the seed is the word; the soils are those who hear)
Captions follow the World English Bible, lightly modernized
check: The hard question’s answer says many scholars think a normal harvest was far smaller than a hundredfold (Genesis 26:12 treats a hundredfold as a blessing). Confirm wording.

The why step says the farmer sows “everywhere” on purpose. Some scholars note that in Galilee sowing could come before plowing, which would explain seed on paths; confirm the lesson does not overstate the farmer’s intent.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever done something good and felt like it went nowhere?
options: then this story is for you. it’s about seed that seems wasted.
i’m sorry. hold that while you listen. the ending is good.
good. keep this for the day it feels that way.

steps.line: So many people came that Jesus got into a boat and sat on the water, while the crowd stood on the shore. He told them a story.
steps.label: Matthew 13:1-3

steps.line: “A farmer went out to sow.” He threw his seed by hand, far and wide.
steps.label: Matthew 13:3

steps.line: Some fell on the path, and birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground. It sprang up fast, then withered in the sun.
steps.label: Matthew 13:4-6

steps.line: Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it.
steps.label: Matthew 13:7

steps.q: So much of his seed is lost. What do you guess happens to the rest?
o: About as much as he sowed, maybe a little more
A harvest up to a hundred times what was sown
steps.why: A huge harvest. The loss is real, and the harvest is bigger.

steps.line: But some fell on good soil, and brought a harvest: a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown.
steps.label: Matthew 13:8

steps.q: Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. What would a farmer then have called a good harvest?
steps.why: Many scholars estimate a good year gave something like tenfold, though estimates vary. A hundredfold sounded like blessing beyond the ordinary: Genesis says Isaac reaped that once.

steps.q: Why would a farmer let seed fall on paths, rocks and thorns?
o: He throws wide, and the good soil makes up for it
He was careless, and Jesus is warning against it
Seed was cheap then, so no one minded
steps.why: Sowers scattered seed by hand, and some scholars think ploughing often came after, so paths and thin soil got seed too. He throws wide and trusts the harvest.

steps.q: Later Jesus explained the soils as kinds of listeners. Match them.
pairs: hears, and it’s snatched away at once
starts with joy, quits when it gets hard
worries and wanting more crowd it out
steps.why: That’s Jesus’s own reading in Mark 4. The good soil hears, takes it in, and bears fruit.

say: here’s what i love. later jesus explains it: the seed is God’s word, and the soils are hearts. some hear and forget, some start fast and quit, some get crowded out by worries.
christians read it two ways: be good soil, and keep sowing kindness and faith, even when most of it seems wasted.

steps.q: In Mark, Jesus asks his friends, “If you don’t understand this story, how will you understand any?” Why this one?
o: It’s the only story he ever explained
It’s the longest one he told
It’s about how you hear all the others
steps.why: Many readers say it’s the key to the rest: every story after it lands on some kind of soil. Before the others begin, this one asks how you’re listening.

today.say: keep throwing seed. do one generous thing today with no guarantee it lands: an encouraging text, a note, a kind word to someone who might shrug it off.
options: good. you won’t always see what grows. the farmer didn’t either.
then they’re your good soil today. throw it.

tomorrow.line: a seed you can barely see, and a pinch of yeast in a mountain of dough.
